source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (reviews Hampton 1987 and later studies)
finding: In classic conjunction studies, truly emergent attributes (true of the combination, not of either part) are rare. Most that appear come from knowing real instances, not from building a new scenario.
numbers: Hampton 1987: strict scoring 3 of 174 attributes emergent; lenient scoring 11. Of 37 attributes unimportant for both parts, about 8% were important for both orders of the conjunction. Pairs with low set overlap (pets/birds) gave more emergence than high overlap (sports/games).
quote: relatively little evidence for creative emergence as a result of problem solving or conflict resolution
limits: Small stimulus sets; attribute listing and rating tasks, not live creative production. Author concludes there is relatively little evidence for creative emergence by problem solving in these conjunctions.
agent_relevance: Emergence is the core claim of blending. Humans show little of it in plain conjunction, so an agent should not assume that merging two sources produces new structure; it must check for it.

source: Hampton (1989, in 1996 review) Conjunctions with a negated constituent
finding: A stricter test of emergence blocks the known-instances route by negating one part (buildings which are not dwellings). Very few attributes emerge, and those come from category stretching.
numbers: Six category pairs, 51 attributes rated 0% for the head noun. 24 stayed at 0% for the conjunction, 11 broke it only slightly (0-5%), only 6 reached 10% or more.
limits: Emergence here is mostly a broadening of the category (a tent counts as a dwelling), not a new idea.
agent_relevance: Separate real emergence from retrieval of a known instance. In an agent, check that a blend property is not just recalled from one source.

source: Hampson (1990, in Hampton 1996) Trait-pair conjunctions
finding: When two personality traits were combined, people inherited behaviours from the parts and produced no emergent behaviours at all.
numbers: Congruent traits: 31 of 32 attributes inherited as expected. Incongruent traits: 16 of 25 likely behaviours inherited, 9 not. Zero emergent attributes in any trait pair.
limits: Reported second hand in a review; small attribute lists.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: incongruent inputs change which features are kept (selective projection) but do not by themselves create new features.

source: Hastie, Schroeder and Weber (1990) and Kunda, Miller and Clare (1990), as reviewed in Hampton (1996): social stereotype conjunctions
finding: Social stereotype conjunctions are a rich source of emergent traits. People explain the contradiction with a scenario, a rule, or a remembered case.
numbers: Hastie et al: emergent ratings (outside the range of both parts by one scale step) on 23% of ratings for congruent and 33% for incongruent conjunctions, 15 bipolar dimensions. Three think-aloud strategies: recall a case, apply a general rule, mentally simulate.
limits: Review-level numbers; the stimuli invite explanation of oddity, so emergence may reflect a demand to explain rather than blending.
agent_relevance: Emergence rises when the combination is incongruent and the reader must explain it. A prompt that asks why the two can coexist may elicit more new structure.

source: Hampton (1996) point-of-view experiment on Socialist Stockbroker type conjunctions
finding: The perspective taken changes the blend strongly. Most inherited attributes came from the other constituent, and about a third of the attributes false of both parts were judged true of the conjunction.
numbers: 210 attributes over four pairs. 65 attributes true of own point of view: 11 (17%) inherited. 80 true of the other category: 55 (69%) inherited. 63 false of both parts: 22 (35%) emergent. Antagonistic pattern in 7 of 8 materials sets in experiment 1. Gender experiment: 12 groups, 8 pairs.
limits: People adopted assigned views rather than being members of the groups; many emergent attributes were obvious (confused, inconsistent).
agent_relevance: Same inputs, different framing, different blend. For the agent: record which perspective drove each blend, and do not treat one run as the blend.

source: Lai, Curran and Menn (2009) Comprehending conventional and novel metaphors: an ERP study (Brain Research 1284)
finding: Replicated the finding that metaphors give larger N400 than literal sentences (Coulson and Van Petten 2002) but with better controlled stimuli showed a time course that depends on conventionality: conventional metaphors converge with literal later, novel ones stay like anomalies.
numbers: 29 right-handed native English speakers, about 25 trials per condition per block (about 400 of 416 trials kept). Reaction times literal 1377 ms < conventional 1487 < novel 1620 = anomalous 1615. Re-analysis excluding items with cloze completion (368 sentences kept) gave the same pattern. Novel metaphors rated low vs high sensicality did not differ (F(1,23)=0.598, p=.45).
limits: ERP difficulty effects do not single out blending; the authors read them as consistent with indirect access and career-of-metaphor accounts. Only partial replication of Tartter 2002 and Arzouan 2007.
agent_relevance: Extra processing cost for novel mappings is real but cannot show that a blended space was built. Do not cite ERP as proof of the blending mechanism.

source: Coulson and Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study (Memory and Cognition)
finding: Original ERP test used as support for blending: sentence endings used literally, as a literal mapping, or metaphorically. N400 was smallest for literal, intermediate for literal mapping, largest for metaphor.
numbers: Ordering literal < literal-mapping < metaphor in N400 amplitude; larger posterior positivity for metaphor. Sample size not read.
limits: Abstract known only through a search summary; page not opened. Lai 2009 replicated the metaphor-over-literal effect.
agent_relevance: Predicts that integration demand, not figurativeness, drives difficulty. Weak support, since confounds are listed.

source: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience (2015) review of metaphor ERP stimulus control, citing Coulson and Van Petten 2002, 2007
finding: Critique: the blending ERP studies controlled the cloze probability of the last word but not the novelty and complexity of the expressions.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Seen only in a search summary.
agent_relevance: One more reason to treat neural evidence for blending as weak.

source: Wulff and Gries (2019) Blend production experiment (lexical blends, Lexis 14)
finding: Three hypotheses from observational data on word blends held up in an experiment, but the main one was weaker.
numbers: 156 students (72 + 84), 4,708 blends, 24 source words. Shorter source contributes more: E1 chi2=266.51, V=0.25, Nagelkerke R2=0.05; E2 chi2=194.7, V=0.1987, R2=0.022. Stress set by second word: 61.5% vs 40.75% baseline (all data), 66.7% vs 36.8% (reduced). Similarity hypothesis: one unexplained simulated-blend trend.
limits: These are LEXICAL blends (portmanteau words), not conceptual integration networks. Weak effects, homogeneous students, 24 words in four domains, marketing-style prompts.
agent_relevance: Shows that observational claims can be tested by production experiments; it does not test emergent structure. Little direct use for the agent.

source: Glebkin (2013) A critical view on conceptual blending theory (CogSci 35)
finding: Argues the theory is a poor account of knowledge creation. Its star examples mostly compress known structure into a form easy to grasp, and the model of composition, completion, elaboration rests on no experimental data.
numbers: No new data. States there is no heated debate and lists objectors: Gibbs 2000, Harder 2003, Brandt 2005, Oakley and Hougaard 2008, Ferguson and Sanford 2008. Calls the complex-numbers example a misunderstanding. Cites de Vega and Urrutia 2011 for sensorimotor anchoring in counterfactual blends.
quote: the model described, however, did not rest on any experimental data
limits: A conceptual critique by one author; the cultural-historical argument (Vygotsky complexes) is contested.
agent_relevance: A blend may help present an idea, not find a true one. Fits the schema rule that a blend is a candidate to be checked by running (G8), never a result.

source: Turner (n.d.) Challenges to blending theory (author reply)
finding: The theory's own proponent concedes the evidence is mostly generalisation over in-sample data tested on out-of-sample data, calls it a framework for a research program, and says outputs are not determined algorithmically from inputs.
numbers: Only experiments named: McCubbins and Turner 2013 (no N or results on the page). Turner 2010 and 2014 survey possible experiments only.
limits: A defender's page; no new numbers.
agent_relevance: No algorithmic recipe exists. An agent must pick inputs and a blend by search plus a check, not by rule.

source: Gibbs (2000/2001) Making good psychology out of blending theory (Cognitive Linguistics 11)
finding: Main psychological critique: the theory gives no testable hypotheses, behaves as a framework, and lets almost anything count as a blend.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Full text paywalled; only citing sources and a search summary read. Year is 2000 or 2001 by citation.
agent_relevance: Supports adding falsifiable tests (a running check) to any blend the agent proposes.

source: Ferguson and Sanford (2008) Anomalies in real and counterfactual worlds (J Memory and Language 58)
finding: Three eye-movement studies: a real-world violation can be neutralised by a counterfactual context, but readers showed early difficulty with real-world violations in every study.
numbers: Counts not read.
limits: Seen through a repository summary; cited by critics, not run as a blending test.
agent_relevance: Even inside a blend, the base world is checked first. An agent should keep a check against the real source constraints.

source: Chan and Schunn (2015) The importance of iteration in creative conceptual combination (Cognition 145)
finding: In a large online innovation platform, the direct effect of far combinations on creativity averaged about zero, but indirect effects (building on concepts that came from far combinations) were more consistently positive.
numbers: Genealogies of many hundreds of concepts over a dozen problems (counts not read).
limits: Abstract known through a search summary only; observational field data.
agent_relevance: A single far combination is not enough. Iterate: build on the blend, and score each generation.

source: Kennedy (2015) University of Alabama thesis: emergence effects in word choice for story generation from conceptual combinations
finding: Stories written from atypical combination seeds were not rated more creative. Creative capacity and working memory did not predict performance.
numbers: Repository abstract gives no N or statistics. LIWC: more verbs, auxiliary verbs, adverbs in atypical-seed stories.
limits: Thesis; only the abstract page read.
agent_relevance: A failure to find the expected benefit of unusual inputs. Treat input distance as a variable to test.

source: Estes and Ward (2002), via search summary: relevance and typicality of modifiers
finding: Relevance and typicality of the modifier were inversely related to emergent attributes, and antonymous and anomalous combinations gave the most emergence.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand summary; the URL is a stand-in (Coulson and Van Petten page); the Estes and Ward page was not opened.
agent_relevance: Anomalous or opposite input pairs give more novelty. Supports choosing distant inputs on purpose.

source: Wilkenfeld and Ward (2001) Similarity and emergence in conceptual combination, via citing sources
finding: Cited for emergence in modification (helicopter blanket gets waterproof, camouflage) and for far combinations giving more novel combinations.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Original abstract not found; second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Same as Estes and Ward: distance helps novelty.

source: Kombine: measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (arXiv 2509.21043)
finding: Blending (find a generic space, build a blend with emergent properties) is the hardest of three tasks for both LLMs and humans. LLMs beat humans on all three.
numbers: 35 LLMs vs 75 Prolific humans (120 recruited), 5 items per task. Mean % of max: LLMs association 59.0, analogy 53.4, blending 43.4; humans 22.1, 32.9, 12.8. Top blending score 64.8 (gpt-5.6-sol); human blending composite 7.4%. Task correlations in LLMs: association-analogy r=0.71, analogy-blending r=0.70, blending-association r=0.54.
limits: LLM judges (Claude Haiku 4.5, o3, GPT-5.4); two inputs only, text only, human sample not expert. Model names as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: Best direct measure of a blend operator in LLMs. Blending needs a valid generic space first; build that as its own step.

source: Kombine (arXiv 2509.21043): abstraction bottleneck and homogeneity
finding: Models find a valid generic space only 43.4% of the time, but once they do, 97.1% of blends are coherent. Blends from different models repeat each other far more than analogies do.
numbers: 2,070 invented concepts; 19.9% (412) reuse at least two properties another model invented for the same item. Blends 14.3x more likely than analogies to repeat 2+ properties (37.3% vs 2.6%). Same-provider models 2.3x more likely to repeat (9.3% vs 4.1%).
limits: Property-overlap measure depends on the embedding and judge.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model collapse onto the same blend (supports guardrail G4). Diversify inputs, not just samples.

source: Kombine (arXiv 2509.21043): judge validity appendix
finding: The LLM-judge panel agrees only moderately with a human.
numbers: One author rated 60 items (30 analogy, 30 blend), 150 dimension judgments: 66% agreement with panel majority, 75% when unanimous (n=96). ICC(2,3) 0.48 to 0.67 over 1,023 artifacts; blend emergent utility lowest at 0.48. Leaderboard ranking stable across encoders (rho >= 0.998).
limits: Human check is one rater.
agent_relevance: Blend scores from model judges are noisy; do not use them as the selection step (guardrail G5). Select by running a check.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in VLMs, CreativeMashup (arXiv 2504.13120)
finding: On a 666-item set of artist-made visual mashups, the best VLMs beat average people at identifying the two inputs and explaining the mashup, but trail experts on the implication.
numbers: 11 VLMs. GPT-4o: identification P/R 75.67/85.00, explanation 74.19, implication win rate 73.5; average people 53.42/70.33, 69.89, 51.0; experts implication 78.3. Claude-3.5-Sonnet 60.08/74.83, 74.19, 62.9. Claude-3-Opus implication 39.2.
limits: Judge is GPT-4o (85.1% and 81.6% agreement with two experts on 200 items); two physical objects, simple backgrounds; text contradicts itself on fusion versus replacement.
agent_relevance: Splitting blend work into identify inputs, find shared attributes, derive implication (IEI) is a usable three-step operator.

source: CreativeMashup (arXiv 2504.13120): generation experiment
finding: Adding the identification-explanation-implication steps to image prompts raised human rank, but artists still won.
numbers: 50 Prolific raters; 5 text-to-image models. IEI beat the shorter two-step prompt for all models (Friedman p<0.0001). Midjourney mean rank 2.40 to 1.98; win rate against experts 0.26 to 0.35. Prompt length 487.95 vs 514.53 words (p=0.404). GPT-4o merged concepts in 36 of 40 DALL-E 3 cases, but 10 of 36 descriptions (27.8%) did not give a satisfying image. SD3-medium gained little.
limits: Gain depends on the image model; GPT-4o writes the prompts.
agent_relevance: Structured blend steps help, and length was ruled out as the cause. The bottleneck can sit downstream of the idea.

source: Li et al. (2025) Is a peeled apple still red? Conceptual combination with property type (CCPT, NAACL 2025)
finding: LLMs struggle to produce noun phrases that have a given emergent property. A spreading-activation prompt helps by a few points.
numbers: 12,315 triplets (2,501 emergent, 1,613 canceled, 8,201 component). 6 LLMs. GPT-4o emergence score: 40.8 induction-emergent, 55.5 canceled, 20.4 noun-phrase completion; with spreading activation (ConceptNet) 45.8, 63.3, 26.9 (+5.0, +7.8, +6.5). Humans 49.2 and 38.0; best base LLM on completion o1 at 32.6.
limits: Test sets are 167 to 200 items; LLM-as-judge (r=0.85 with humans on 300 pairs); annotators from a narrow demographic.
agent_relevance: Emergence is hard for LLMs even for noun phrases; add a retrieval-of-associations step before blending.

source: CCPT (NAACL 2025): property-type classification
finding: GPT-4o decides if a property is present (82.6%) but identifies its type poorly.
numbers: 1,000 samples. Property type accuracy 56.4% vs 81% humans: emergent 90.0%, component 37.2%, canceled 45.2%, others 53.2%. Ablation: removing the filter cost 1.2, 7.7 and 0.9 points.
limits: Single model for classification.
agent_relevance: A model cannot reliably tell a new property from an inherited one, so novelty of a blend should be checked by code against the source lists.

source: Gu, Wang, Zhang and Li (2025) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity (arXiv 2412.14141)
finding: A pipeline that retrieves across abstraction levels and recombines gave ideas closer to real follow-up work than direct generation.
numbers: 87 OAG-Bench papers, Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Mean embedding similarity: design rationale 0.85 vs 0.78, universal principle 0.83 vs 0.75, key mechanism 0.87 vs 0.77 (abstract: 7 to 10%).
limits: Similarity to a published paper with SPECTER embeddings, one model, no human raters, no variance or test statistics, hand-chosen cases.
agent_relevance: Retrieving at higher abstraction (a generic space) before combining is a sensible design, but evidence is thin.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2025) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? (ICLR 2025)
finding: Blind experts rated LLM ideas as more novel but not more feasible; idea diversity collapsed and LLM judges failed.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty 1-10: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p<0.01), AI reranked by human 5.81 (p<0.001). Feasibility 6.61 / 6.34 / 6.44 (n.s.). 4,000 seeds per topic, only about 5% non-duplicate at cosine 0.8. Reviewer agreement: LLM judges 43.3% to 53.3% vs human reviewers 56.1%.
limits: Not a blending test; combination was not isolated. Ideas written by experts under time limits.
agent_relevance: Novelty is cheap and diversity is the limit. Use code to dedupe and a run to check feasibility.

source: Olearo et al. (2026) Blending concepts with text-to-image diffusion models (arXiv 2506.23630)
finding: Four inference-time blending methods for diffusion; switching and alternating prompts won, embedding interpolation was worst.
numbers: 100 adults aged 19-25, 22 concept pairs, Stable Diffusion 1.4. Preference: alternate > textual 0.60, alternate > switch 0.51 (p=0.31, tied), switch > textual 0.61. Failures: first concept dominates, flat colours, order sensitivity.
limits: Best seed hand-picked from 10; short prompts; one model; paper counts are inconsistent (four vs five categories, 84 vs 88 images).
agent_relevance: Blend results depend on order and seed; test both orders.

source: Blending Concepts: VMetaphor-Bench (arXiv 2609.02502)
finding: Text-to-image models know the domains but fail at structure and mapping, mainly with replacement blends.
numbers: 1,500 images, 11 models. Top GPT Image 1.5 MCQ 85.4 (structure 78.1, mapping 76.5), bottom OmniGen2 61.4. Replacement accuracy 18.9% vs fusion 67.9% and juxtaposition 69.2%. Descriptive prompts add +3.1 to +16.6 points. Cross-judge rho 0.991. Human check: 5 annotators, 200 images, 80.24% balanced accuracy.
limits: Judge is an MLLM; Western-skewed; human check covers 2 of 11 models.
agent_relevance: Spelling out the intended blend structure in the prompt closes much of the gap. Name the blend type.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models (conceptual analysis)
finding: Theoretical: human blends are driven by embodied goals, LLM blends are distributionally novel with proxy-goals from training and prompts.
numbers: No original numbers or tests.
limits: Neither account is tested.
agent_relevance: Argues the choice of goal is what the agent lacks: supply the goal in the blend slot.

source: Sato (2025) The way we prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics, and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs (arXiv 2505.10948)
finding: Uses blending theory as a frame for prompt-induced transitions and hallucinations.
numbers: Abstract has no numbers or models. A search summary claims LLMs showed no difference between fused and non-fused prompts; not verified.
limits: Abstract only; weak.
agent_relevance: No usable effect size.

source: Xi, Cheng, Soni and Turner (2026) Evaluating creative generative AI with conceptual blending (ACL 2026 EvalEval poster)
finding: Position: score creativity by how well outputs integrate two domains into emergent structure, over FrameNet frames; rubric dimensions include understanding depth and coherence.
numbers: No experiment or numbers on the poster.
limits: Poster text partly truncated.
agent_relevance: A rubric to test blends by code.
